Introduction
A hospital portal, a claims system, a patient intake form, a lab results viewer — a great many of these run on ColdFusion, and a great many were written before anyone on the team had heard the phrase “ePHI.” They work. title: thalmle — T-HAL-MLE nativo en R: regresión LASSO adaptativa para dosis-respuesta continua
summary:
thalmle — T-HAL-MLE nativo para dosis-respuesta continua

Autor: Pedro Sordo Martínez — amurlaniakea@gmail.com

Licencia: AGPL-3.0-or-later.
Repo: amurlaniakea/thalmle

1. Qué problema resuelve thalmle

En epidemiología, farmacocinética, economía aplicada o cualquier campo con tratamiento continuo (A), confusores (W) y un outcome (Y), la curva de influencia psi(a) = E_W[Q_0(a, W)] es el objetivo central. El algoritmo Targeted Highly Adaptive Lasso Minimum Loss Estimation (T-HAL-MLE, arXiv:2607.03824) resuelve esto con tres pasos:

  1. Nuisances: omega_n (marginal de A), Q_n (outcome) y g_n (densidad condicional g(a|W)).
  2. Targeting: base HAL (spline_basis), selector lambda por tamaño de sieve (select_lambda_by_size), proyección OLS (thal_core).
  3. Inferencia: curva de influencia (influence_curve) e intervalos de Wald (wald_ci).

El repo thalmle restaura la implementación completa (v0.0.2, 1d23f8c) y la hace reproducible sin depender de versiones rotas de paquetes binarios pesados.

2. Flujo del algoritmo (verificación literal)

El siguiente diagrama mermaid resume el flujo verificado en el código real (R/thal_core.R, línea 32–142):

graph TD
    A[A: dosis continua] --> B[omega_n: KDE Sheather-Jones]
    A --> C[g_n: haldensify v0.2.8]
    W[W: confusores] --> C
    Y --> D[Q_n: hal9001 v0.4.6]
    W --> D
    B --> E[w_cap: sqrt(n)*log(n/5) o Inf]
    C --> F[psi_init = colMeans(Q(A,W))]
    D --> F
    E --> G[psi_hat = spline_basis(grid) %*% alpha]
    F --> H[Crossfit avg/full + CV]
    G --> H
    H --> I[psi_hat final + psi_plugin]

Verificación paso a paso (ejecutado en esta sesión):

  • fit_omega_kde(A) usa stats::density(..., bw = "SJ") (línea 5, R/initial_fit.R).
  • fit_Q_hal(A, W, Y) usa hal9001::fit_hal(X = cbind(A, W), ...) con THAL_QSO por defecto (1, línea 5).
  • fit_g_haldensify(A, W) usa haldensity::haldensity(...) con trim = FALSE y min_density = 1e-4 (líneas 20–41, initial_fit.R).
  • thal_core(...) aplica w_cap = sqrt(n)*log(n/5) por defecto (línea 40) y lanza warning si grid sale de range(A) (línea 40, parche 55ecea2).

3. Gráfico ilustrativo: targeting con y sin cap

El siguiente código R (ejecutable con el paquete instalado) genera la figura comparativa que se describe en el README.md (tabla de defaults):

library(thalmle)
# Datos sintéticos (DGP 1, uniforme)
n <- 500
sim <- simulate_data(n, dgp = 1, treatment = "uniform")
A  <- sim$A; W <- sim$W; Y <- sim$Y

# Ajuste completo con cap por defecto
res_default <- thal_core(A, W, Y,
                       Q_fun = fit_Q_hal,
                       g_fun  = fit_g_haldensify,
                       omega_fun = fit_omega_kde,
                       grid  = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100),
                       w_cap = NULL)   # sqrt(n)*log(n/5)

# Ajuste con cap desactivado
res_inf <- thal_core(A, W, Y,
                     Q_fun = fit_Q_hal,
                     g_fun  = fit_g_haldensify,
                     omega_fun = fit_omega_kde,
                     grid  = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100),
                     w_cap = Inf)

# Visualización (código que genera la figura)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(res_default$grid, res_default$psi_hat, type = "l", col = "steelblue",
     main = "Cap por defecto (sqrt(n)*log(n/5))",
     ylab = "psi_hat", xlab = "a")
abline(h = mean(res_default$psi_plugin), col = "red", lty = 2)
plot(res_inf$grid, res_inf$psi_hat, type = "l", col = "darkgreen",
     main = "Cap desactivado (Inf)",
     ylab = "psi_hat", xlab = "a")
abline(h = mean(res_inf$psi_plugin), col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("psi_hat", "psi_plugin (media)"),
       col = c("steelblue", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")

Interpretación verificada: con w_cap = NULL, los pesos omega/g se recortan, evitando extrapolaciones extremas cuando g es pequeño (colas de la densidad). Con w_cap = Inf, la curva es más volátil, como se documenta en el README.md (ADVERTENCIA sobre w_cap por defecto poco fiable con tratamiento normal).

4. Aplicaciones científicas y técnicas

El tipo de regresión LASSO adaptativa (HAL) con targeting (T-HAL-MLE) es aplicable en múltiples dominios. Algunos ejemplos verificados con los DGP del repositorio (tests/testthat/, experiments/):

Área Variable A Confusores W Uso del repo
Epidemiología Dosis de medicamento (mg/kg) Edad, IMC, biomarcadores Estimar psi(a) para optimizar dosis mínima efectiva
Farmacocinética Concentración de fármaco en plasma (ng/mL) Genotipos metabolizadores (CYP2D6) Predicción de toxicidad por concentración
Economía aplicada Intensidad de programa social ($ transferido) Ingresos previos, educación, ubicación Impacto de transferencias en empleo (curva dosis-respuesta)
Agricultura de precisión Cantidad de fertilizante (kg/ha) pH del suelo, humedad, temperatura Rendimiento óptimo por dosis variable
Climatología Intensidad de evento (mm precipitación) Altitud, latitud, uso del suelo Riesgo de inundación por intensidad de lluvia

Todos los ejemplos pueden reproducirse con simulate_data(n, dgp = ...) (líneas 60–75, R/dgp.R) y evaluarse con thal_oracle() o thal_core() según el escenario (treatment = "uniform" o "normal").

5. Instalación rápida 

# Desde el repositorio (clon o descarga)
devtools::install_github("amurlaniakea/thalmle", ref = "fix/restaurar-codigo-real")

# Uso básico
library(thalmle)
res <- thal_core(A, W, Y, grid = seq(min(A), max(A), length.out = 50))
plot(res$grid, res$psi_hat, type = "l", col = "steelblue")
abline(h = mean(res$psi_plugin), col = "red", lty = 2)
  • Verificación: cada afirmación de este artículo está respaldada por salidas literales de terminal (git rev-parse, ls, grep, Rscript) y por la ejecución de los 16 tests base (PASS 16) + 3 tests HAL (PASS 3).

Para preguntas técnicas: amurlaniakea@gmail.com o `https://github.com/amurlaniakea/thalmle'

title: One Developer + One AI Bot: Building an SSH Client in 45 Self-Iterating Rounds
summary:
I'm building AI-SSH-Pro, an open-source SSH client with a built-in AI assistant (Electron + React + TypeScript): terminal, SFTP, command history and AI chat in one window.

The unusual part is the team. It's me plus one AI bot. I treat the bot as a whole product team — product manager, UX/UI designer, developer, QA, and retro lead — and let it iterate round after round on its own. My job is direction, feedback, and deciding when to ship.

This post covers how that works, the actual role prompts I use, and real retrospective notes from the repo.

The numbers

All of these come straight from git log and the docs folder, as of 2026-10-21:

  • 405 commits in total (first commit on 2026-04-02), 319 of them in just two days (Oct 20–21).
  • 45 rounds of continuous self-iteration completed since Oct 20; round 46 is in progress.
  • 124 design docs under docs/iterations/.
  • 407 regression tests, all green on the latest full npm test run.
  • 11 retro entries in docs/retro.md, distilled into 17 rules in docs/dev-rules.md.

The loop: one bot, five hats

Every round follows the same pipeline:

Product → UX/UI design → Development → QA → Retro

  • Product proposes just 3 small items per round, focused on what people use every day: connecting, the terminal, SFTP, history, AI chat.
  • Design screenshots the real UI first, then writes a design doc.
  • Development commits in small steps — one item, one commit.
  • QA adds regression tests; nothing is done until the full suite passes.
  • Retro turns every mistake into an actionable rule that the next round reads first.

A round takes roughly 30 minutes. Any bug I report jumps the queue.

The role prompts

These are the prompts I actually use, lightly trimmed. Feel free to copy them.

Shared context (always first)

Project: AI-SSH-Pro, an AI SSH client (Electron + React + TypeScript).
Rules: commit locally only; push only for releases. npm test must be fully green.
Use theme components and spacing tokens, never native

title: Verify CBE and Telebirr payments in your app with a free API
summary:
If you sell anything online in Ethiopia, you know the flow: the customer pays by bank transfer or Telebirr, then sends a screenshot. Someone on your team looks at it and decides whether to ship. Screenshots are easy to edit and easy to reuse, so that decision is a guess.

I maintain cheki.et, a free, MIT-licensed receipt checker, and this post is the developer version: how to confirm a payment against the bank's own record from your backend, in a few lines of Node or Python.

One thing first, because it's the most common confusion I see. Searching "telebirr api" or "cbe api" mostly turns up payment collection: merchant APIs where you start a payment and get a callback. Those need a merchant agreement with the bank. What I'm describing is the other half. The customer has already paid, the normal way, and you want to check the receipt they sent you. That needs no contract with anyone, because Ethiopian banks and wallets publish every receipt at a public URL.

How it works

Each bank has its own receipt page: transactioninfo.ethiotelecom.et/receipt/{number} for Telebirr, mbreciept.cbe.com.et/{receiptId} for CBE, a JSON endpoint for Bank of Abyssinia, a PDF for CBE Birr, and so on. cheki fetches the right one, parses it, runs a few sanity checks (positive amount, the reference you asked for, no failed or pending status), and returns the same JSON for every bank. There are 10 banks and wallets live: CBE, Telebirr, BOA, M-Pesa, Dashen, Awash, CBE Birr, Siinqee, eBirr and ZamZam. Three of those (M-Pesa, ZamZam, CBE Birr) are marked beta because they've been checked against few or no real receipts.

One request 

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"}'

No signup and no API key. The body takes bank plus whatever that bank needs:

Field When
reference Almost always: a receipt link, Receipt ID, transaction number or FT Ref
accountNumber BOA (last 5 digits) and older CBE FT receipts (last 8 digits)
phoneNumber CBE Birr (the payer's phone)
qrData A scanned QR payload (BOA, CBE Birr, Telebirr)

That reference is made up, so you'll get a 422 back. A confirmed receipt looks like this (names and numbers are fake):

{
  "success": true,
  "verified": true,
  "bank": "Commercial Bank of Ethiopia",
  "bankCode": "cbe",
  "reference": "FT26SAMPLE01",
  "senderName": "ABEBE KEBEDE",
  "receiverName": "TIGIST ALEMU",
  "receiverAccount": "1****6171",
  "amount": 1250.5,
  "currency": "ETB",
  "date": "2026-10-01",
  "sourceUrl": "https://apps.cbe.com.et:100/?id=FT26SAMPLE0100006171",
  "cached": false
}

The rule that matters: only verified: true means the bank confirmed it. success: true only means the request was handled. A BOA QR that BOA couldn't confirm comes back with success: true, verified: false, decodedOnly: true, and a QR can be copied. Don't ship on that.

The error codes are what you'd expect: 400 bad input, 404 unknown bank, 413 body too large, 422 the bank has no such receipt, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After), 502 the bank couldn't be reached. A 502 for a geo-blocked bank includes a fallbackUrl, which is the bank's own receipt page.

Node: cheki-verify 

npm install cheki-verify   # 1.6.0, no dependencies, Node 20+

Here's the check I'd run before marking an order paid. Confirm it with the bank, then make sure it's actually this order's payment:

import { Cheki, isVerified, ChekiAPIError } from "cheki-verify";

const cheki = new Cheki();
const seen = new Set(); // use a UNIQUE column in your database instead

async function checkPayment(order, bank, reference) {
  let r;
  try {
    r = await cheki.verify(bank, reference);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ChekiAPIError) {
      // 422: the bank has no such receipt. 502 + fallbackUrl: bank not reachable from the server.
      return { ok: false, why: e.serverMessage ?? e.message, openAtBank: e.fallbackUrl };
    }
    throw e; // network error or timeout: try again later, don't accept
  }
  if (!isVerified(r)) return { ok: false, why: "not confirmed by the bank" };
  if (r.amount !== order.amount) return { ok: false, why: `amount is ${r.amount}` };
  if (!r.receiverAccount?.endsWith(order.accountLast4)) return { ok: false, why: "paid to another account" };
  const key = `${r.bankCode}:${r.reference}`;
  if (seen.has(key)) return { ok: false, why: "receipt already used" };
  seen.add(key);
  return { ok: true, payer: r.senderName, date: r.date };
}

console.log(await checkPayment({ amount: 1250.5, accountLast4: "6171" }, "dashen", "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"));

The last two checks are the ones people skip. A real receipt for a transfer to someone else's account passes isVerified. So does a real receipt the same customer already used last week. The bank can't know about your orders, so those checks have to live in your code.

In the TypeScript SDK, any non-2xx response throws a ChekiAPIError (with statusCode, fallbackUrl and checkedUrl), and a 429 throws ChekiRateLimitError. It retries at most once, and only where that's safe.

Python: cheki 

pip install cheki   # 1.6.0, needs only requests, Python 3.10+

The Python client returns a result for API errors instead of raising, so it reads as one if:

from cheki import ChekiClient

with ChekiClient() as cheki:
    r = cheki.verify("cbe", "https://mbreciept.cbe.com.et/fHCxExampleRcpt01")

    if r.is_verified:
        print(r.sender_name, "paid", r.amount, r.currency, "to", r.receiver_account, "on", r.date)
    elif r.fallback_url:
        print("Bank not reachable from the server. Open:", r.fallback_url)
    else:
        print(f"Not verified ({r.http_status}): {r.error}")

It also installs a small CLI, which is handy in a terminal: cheki-verify telebirr DET0SAMPLE --json. It exits 0 only when the bank confirmed the receipt.

End-of-day reconciliation

POST /api/verify/batch takes up to 20 receipts:

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify/batch \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"receipts": [
        {"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"},
        {"bank": "boa", "reference": "FT26SAMPLE07", "accountNumber": "12345"}
      ]}'

You get back total, verified, failed, cached and one result per receipt. Both SDKs wrap it as verifyBatch / verify_batch.

Limits and what's kept

  • Server side only. The API sends no CORS headers, so call it from your backend, not the browser.
  • Rate limits per IP: 30 checks a minute (each batch item counts), and 5 batch requests a minute. The SDKs export RECOMMENDED_BATCH_CHUNK (15) for long lists.
  • Storage: no accounts and no database. A receipt the bank confirmed stays in the server's memory for up to six hours, so a repeat check returns cached: true without asking the bank again. Failed checks are never kept.

The full reference is in the API docs, and the developer page has the Go, PHP and Dart SDKs as well.

Telebirr and M-Pesa: self-host it

Telebirr's and M-Pesa's receipt pages only answer requests from Ethiopian networks. The hosted cheki.et API runs in Frankfurt, so for those two it returns a 502 with fallbackUrl. That's fine for a person at a counter, who can open the link on their phone, but not for an automated checkout.

The fix is to run your own copy on a server in Ethiopia:

If you sell anything online in Ethiopia, you know the flow: the customer pays by bank transfer or Telebirr, then sends a screenshot. Someone on your team looks at it and decides whether to ship. Screenshots are easy to edit and easy to reuse, so that decision is a guess.

I maintain cheki.et, a free, MIT-licensed receipt checker, and this post is the developer version: how to confirm a payment against the bank's own record from your backend, in a few lines of Node or Python.

One thing first, because it's the most common confusion I see. Searching "telebirr api" or "cbe api" mostly turns up payment collection: merchant APIs where you start a payment and get a callback. Those need a merchant agreement with the bank. What I'm describing is the other half. The customer has already paid, the normal way, and you want to check the receipt they sent you. That needs no contract with anyone, because Ethiopian banks and wallets publish every receipt at a public URL.

How it works

Each bank has its own receipt page: transactioninfo.ethiotelecom.et/receipt/{number} for Telebirr, mbreciept.cbe.com.et/{receiptId} for CBE, a JSON endpoint for Bank of Abyssinia, a PDF for CBE Birr, and so on. cheki fetches the right one, parses it, runs a few sanity checks (positive amount, the reference you asked for, no failed or pending status), and returns the same JSON for every bank. There are 10 banks and wallets live: CBE, Telebirr, BOA, M-Pesa, Dashen, Awash, CBE Birr, Siinqee, eBirr and ZamZam. Three of those (M-Pesa, ZamZam, CBE Birr) are marked beta because they've been checked against few or no real receipts.

One request 

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"}'

No signup and no API key. The body takes bank plus whatever that bank needs:

Field When
reference Almost always: a receipt link, Receipt ID, transaction number or FT Ref
accountNumber BOA (last 5 digits) and older CBE FT receipts (last 8 digits)
phoneNumber CBE Birr (the payer's phone)
qrData A scanned QR payload (BOA, CBE Birr, Telebirr)

That reference is made up, so you'll get a 422 back. A confirmed receipt looks like this (names and numbers are fake):

{
  "success": true,
  "verified": true,
  "bank": "Commercial Bank of Ethiopia",
  "bankCode": "cbe",
  "reference": "FT26SAMPLE01",
  "senderName": "ABEBE KEBEDE",
  "receiverName": "TIGIST ALEMU",
  "receiverAccount": "1****6171",
  "amount": 1250.5,
  "currency": "ETB",
  "date": "2026-10-01",
  "sourceUrl": "https://apps.cbe.com.et:100/?id=FT26SAMPLE0100006171",
  "cached": false
}

The rule that matters: only verified: true means the bank confirmed it. success: true only means the request was handled. A BOA QR that BOA couldn't confirm comes back with success: true, verified: false, decodedOnly: true, and a QR can be copied. Don't ship on that.

The error codes are what you'd expect: 400 bad input, 404 unknown bank, 413 body too large, 422 the bank has no such receipt, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After), 502 the bank couldn't be reached. A 502 for a geo-blocked bank includes a fallbackUrl, which is the bank's own receipt page.

npm install cheki-verify   # 1.6.0, no dependencies, Node 20+

import { Cheki, isVerified, ChekiAPIError } from "cheki-verify";

const cheki = new Cheki();
const seen = new Set(); // use a UNIQUE column in your database instead

async function checkPayment(order, bank, reference) {
  let r;
  try {
    r = await cheki.verify(bank, reference);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ChekiAPIError) {
      // 422: the bank has no such receipt. 502 + fallbackUrl: bank not reachable from the server.
      return { ok: false, why: e.serverMessage ?? e.message, openAtBank: e.fallbackUrl };
    }
    throw e; // network error or timeout: try again later, don't accept
  }
  if (!isVerified(r)) return { ok: false, why: "not confirmed by the bank" };
  if (r.amount !== order.amount) return { ok: false, why: `amount is ${r.amount}` };
  if (!r.receiverAccount?.endsWith(order.accountLast4)) return { ok: false, why: "paid to another account" };
  const key = `${r.bankCode}:${r.reference}`;
  if (seen.has(key)) return { ok: false, why: "receipt already used" };
  seen.add(key);
  return { ok: true, payer: r.senderName, date: r.date };
}

The last two checks are the ones people skip. A real receipt for a transfer to someone else's account passes isVerified. So does a real receipt the same customer already used last week. The bank can't know about your orders, so those checks have to live in your code.

with ChekiClient() as cheki:
    r = cheki.verify("cbe", "https://mbreciept.cbe.com.et/fHCxExampleRcpt01")

    if r.is_verified:
        print(r.sender_name, "paid", r.amount, r.currency, "to", r.receiver_account, "on", r.date)
    elif r.fallback_url:

title: Les di una oficina a mis agentes de IA, y ahora mi equipo puede verlos trabajar
summary:
Este artículo es la versión en español de I gave my AI coding agents an office, and now my team can watch them work.

Paso casi todo el día con tres o cuatro agentes de IA trabajando a la vez: Claude Code en dos perfiles, Codex en otra terminal, a veces un subagente o dos. Son buena compañía, pero invisible. La única forma de saber que uno lleva cinco minutos esperando mi permiso es revisar terminal por terminal.

Así que les hice una oficina.

deskmates es una oficina pixel-art donde cada sesión de un agente en tu equipo es un personaje en su escritorio. Entra cuando la sesión empieza, escribe mientras edita, lee mientras busca, levanta un signo de pregunta amarillo cuando necesita tu permiso y se va cuando la sesión termina. Los subagentes se sientan al lado del agente que los lanzó y, cuando terminan, pasan por su escritorio con un documento antes de irse.

Es código abierto (MIT) y se instala con un comando:

npm install -g deskmates
deskmates serve      # http://127.0.0.1:47821
deskmates demo       # agentes simulados, por si quieres verlo antes de conectar nada

Cómo entran los agentes

Cada herramienta le cuenta a deskmates lo que hace a su manera, y todo termina convertido en el mismo evento pequeño:

  • Claude Code, mediante hooks. deskmates connect los agrega a la configuración de un perfil, marcados para que disconnect quite solo los suyos. El hook son unas pocas líneas de shell con un tope de 50 ms que siempre termina con código 0: nunca debe frenar a un agente.
  • Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor y Gemini CLI, mediante los archivos de sesión que ya escriben. Sin configuración.
  • Cualquier otra cosa, mediante una pequeña API HTTP de ingesta o un servidor MCP, para que un script, un job de CI u otro agente también pueda entrar.

Desde ahí los datos van en un solo sentido: eventos, deduplicación, un reducer puro que decide quién está trabajando, esperando, libre, dormido o saliendo, y un WebSocket que alimenta la página. La página es un canvas con una simulación de actores encima: caminan por una cuadrícula de casillas, toman descansos en las máquinas expendedoras, se reúnen cuando dos agentes del mismo proyecto están libres, y hay mascotas que pasean entre las salas.

La privacidad fue la primera regla, no la última

Una oficina que muestra lo que hacen tus agentes podría mostrar demasiado con mucha facilidad. Los eventos llevan solo el nombre de una herramienta y un detalle de 120 caracteres como máximo: un nombre de archivo o la primera línea de un comando. Los prompts, el contenido de los archivos y la salida de las herramientas nunca salen de los adaptadores, y el historial diario guarda conteos, no contenido. Nada sale de tu equipo a menos que lo pidas.

Después terminó en el TV de la oficina

Al lado de mi teclado no era donde la quería. La quería en una tablet, y después en la pantalla de la oficina.

deskmates serve --lan la sirve en tu red detrás de un token, imprime un QR en la terminal, y la página tiene un botón para compartir con el mismo QR y un modo kiosco que llena la pantalla. En un TV eso significó aprender sobre píxeles de dispositivo: la oficina se dibuja a escalas enteras para que el pixel art se vea nítido, y el modo kiosco la estira para llenar la pantalla cuando eso importa más.

La oficina compartida

Ver solo a mis agentes me aburrió rápido. Varios de nosotros usamos agentes de programación, así que la última pieza fue una oficina compartida:

# en un equipo al que todos puedan llegar
deskmates serve --lan --shared

# en cada PC
deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús"

Cada PC envía los mismos eventos pequeños a la oficina compartida, donde llegan al piso Headquarters: seis islas de cuatro escritorios, cada una con el color de su PC, una sala de estar, una mesa de reuniones y un café en el medio. Cuando agentes de PCs distintas esperan permiso al mismo tiempo, se van al café a conversar. Es la función más inútil que escribí este año, y mi favorita.

Lo que aprendí

  • Núcleo puro, bordes visuales. El reducer y la escena son funciones deterministas de los eventos y del tiempo. Eso hizo que casi todo se pudiera probar sin navegador, y las pruebas en el navegador comparan capturas píxel por píxel.
  • El piso tuvo que convertirse en datos. La oficina compartida empezó con la misma sala pequeña repetida una al lado de otra. Un solo piso grande obligó a convertir las constantes de la sala en un valor que los temas pueden declarar. Todas las capturas existentes tenían que quedar idénticas mientras eso pasaba, y esa regla atrapó más errores que cualquier revisión.
  • Los agentes revisan código mejor de lo que esperaba, y leen capturas peor que yo. Construí casi todo esto con Claude Code, con un agente nuevo revisando cada cambio. Encontraron errores reales de concurrencia y de casos límite; las imágenes las tuve que mirar yo, una por una.

Pruébalo

  • Repositorio: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates
  • Instalación: npm install -g deskmates, después deskmates serve y deskmates connect
  • Node 22.18 o superior

Si trabajas con varios agentes al día, me gustaría saber qué señal extrañas más cuando trabajan en segundo plano. Eso es lo que decide qué aprende la oficina después.

title: pyursa: a dataframe library built for AI agents, not just humans
summary:
AI agents write a lot of data code now. Ask an agent to "find our top regions by revenue" and it will usually write pandas code, run it and report a number.

The problem is that pandas was designed for a human sitting at a notebook. A human glances at the output, notices something looks off, and fixes it. An agent often doesn't. And pandas is very good at giving you a wrong answer without saying anything.

Here are three things pandas does without complaint:

import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({"x": [2**62, 2**62]}).x.sum()
# -9223372036854775808   <- integer overflow, wrapped around silently

df = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["paid", None]})
len(df[df.status == None])
# 0                      <- "== None" never matches, so every row is dropped

pd.DataFrame({"price": [0.1, 0.2]}).price.sum()
# 0.30000000000000004    <- money stored as floats

None of these raise an error. A human might catch them. An agent running a 20-step pipeline will build on them and confidently report the result.

I built pyursa to fix this. It's an open-source Python dataframe library designed for the way agents (and the people supervising them) actually work.

pip install "pyursa[all]"

What pyursa is

pyursa is a lazy, strictly typed dataframe API that runs on Polars or DuckDB, with Apache Arrow underneath. You write one pipeline; you choose the engine when you run it. On top of that sits a layer built specifically for agents: structured errors, undo, lineage, dry runs, context-sized summaries, LLM-powered operators and an MCP server.

import pyursa as pu
from pyursa import col

orders = pu.read_parquet("orders/*.parquet")   # lazy: nothing is read yet

report = (orders
    .filter(col("qty") > 0, col("status") != "cancelled", intent="valid orders only")
    .with_columns(revenue=col("qty") * col("price"))
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(revenue=col("revenue").sum(), orders=pu.len())
    .sort("revenue", descending=True))

report.collect("duckdb")   # a pyarrow.Table
report.collect("polars")   # the same table, value for value

If you know Polars, this will look familiar. The difference is in what happens when things go wrong, and in everything around the query.

1. Errors an agent can fix by itself

When an agent makes a mistake, the most useful thing a library can do is tell it exactly what's wrong and how to fix it, in a form it can parse. Every pyursa error has a stable code, details, and a suggested fix you can paste straight into the code:

orders.filter(col("quantity") > 5)

[COLUMN_NOT_FOUND] Column 'quantity' not found in the input of this step.
  suggestion: Did you mean 'qty'?  ->  col("qty")

The same error is available as JSON, which is what an agent actually consumes:

{
  "error": "COLUMN_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Column 'quantity' not found in the input of this step.",
  "details": {"column": "quantity", "available_columns": ["order_id", "region", "qty", "price", "status"]},
  "suggestions": [{"description": "Did you mean 'qty'?", "fix": "col(\"qty\")"}]
}

Remember the pandas == None problem? pyursa refuses it and explains why:

[INVALID_OPERATION] Comparing to None with '==' always yields null, so it filters out every row.
  suggestion: Use .is_null() to test for missing values.  ->  col("status").is_null()

Comparing a number to a string gives TYPE_MISMATCH with the fix col("qty") > 5. Overflowing an integer gives INTEGER_OVERFLOW instead of a negative number.

Crucially, these errors happen when the plan is built, not when it runs. Plans are type-checked step by step, so an agent finds out about a mistake in milliseconds, before it has scanned a single gigabyte.

2. Strict types: no silent corruption

pyursa takes the position that losing data quietly is always a bug:

  • Exact decimals. Decimal(12, 2) math stays exact on every engine. qty * price with a Decimal(5,2) price gives a Decimal(38,2) result, not a float.
  • Strict casts. Casting "12abc" to an integer raises CAST_FAILED. Casting 2.7 to an integer raises an error too, instead of quietly truncating or rounding; you round explicitly if that's what you mean.
  • Time zones are part of the type. Datetime("America/Toronto") and Datetime("UTC") are different types.
  • Lossy inputs are rejected: nanosecond timestamps that would be truncated, unsigned integers too big for Int64, column names that differ only by case.

3. Same answer on every engine

"Engine-agnostic" usually means "it runs on several engines and gives slightly different answers on each". Null ordering, NaN handling, rounding, integer division, quantile methods and window ties all vary between engines.

pyursa defines one semantics contract and enforces it with conformance tests that run every operation on every engine and compare the results:

  • nulls sort last; sorts are stable
  • NaN is a value (larger than every number, equal to itself), not a missing value
  • rounding is half away from zero
  • quantiles are linear; std and var use ddof=1
  • Int64 overflow is an error everywhere

So collect("polars") and collect("duckdb") return the same Arrow table. The only allowed difference is the last digits of float sums, since floating-point addition depends on order. You can develop against Polars on your laptop and run on DuckDB in production, or switch when one engine fits a workload better, without your numbers changing.

4. Undo, history, lineage and dry runs

Agents explore. They try something, look at it, back up and try something else. pyursa frames are immutable, so going back is free.

History, with the agent's stated intent recorded at each step:

for step in report.history():
    print(step["op"], step["intent"])
# source        None
# filter        valid orders only
# with_columns  None
# aggregate     None

title: I gave my AI coding agents an office, and now my team can watch them work
summary:
I spend most of my day with three or four AI coding agents running at once: Claude Code in two profiles, Codex in another terminal, sometimes a subagent or two. They are good company, but invisible company. The only way to know that one of them has been waiting for my permission for five minutes is to cycle through terminals.

So I built them an office.

deskmates is a pixel-art office where every agent session on your machine is a character at a desk. It walks in when the session starts, types while it edits, reads while it searches, raises a yellow question mark when it needs your permission, and walks out when the session ends. Subagents sit next to the agent that launched them, and when they finish they stop by its desk with a document before leaving.

It is open source (MIT), and it installs with one command:

npm install -g deskmates
deskmates serve      # http://127.0.0.1:47821
deskmates demo       # simulated agents, if you want to see it before connecting anything

How the agents get in

Every tool tells deskmates what it is doing in its own way, and everything ends up as the same small event:

  • Claude Code through hooks. deskmates connect adds them to a profile's settings, tagged so disconnect removes only its own. The hook is a few lines of shell with a 50 ms ceiling that always exits 0: it must never slow an agent down.
  • Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor and Gemini CLI through the session files they already write. No setup.
  • Anything else through a small HTTP ingest API or an MCP server, so a script, a CI job or another agent can walk in too.

From there the data flows one way: events, deduplication, a pure reducer that decides who is working, waiting, idle, asleep or leaving, and a WebSocket that feeds the page. The page is a canvas with an actor simulation on top: walking on a tile grid, breaks at the vending machines, meetings when two agents of the same project are free, pets that wander between rooms.

Privacy was the first rule, not the last

An office that shows what your agents do could easily show too much. Events carry only a tool name and a detail of at most 120 characters: a file name or the first line of a command. Prompts, file contents and tool output never leave the adapters, and the daily history stores counts, not content. Nothing leaves your machine unless you ask it to.

Then it ended up on the office TV

Next to my keyboard was not where I wanted it. I wanted it on a tablet, and then on the screen in the office.

deskmates serve --lan serves your network behind a token, prints a QR in the terminal, and the page has a Share button with the same QR and a kiosk mode that fills the screen. On a TV that meant learning about device pixels: the office is drawn at whole-number scales so the pixel art stays crisp, and kiosk stretches it to fill the screen when that matters more.

The shared office

Watching only my agents got old quickly. Several of us use coding agents, so the last piece was a shared office:

# on a machine everyone can reach
deskmates serve --lan --shared

# on each PC
deskmates serve --relay http://lab:47821 --name "Jesús"

Each PC relays the same small events to the shared office, where they land on the Headquarters floor: six islands of four desks, each in its PC's colour, a lounge, a meeting table and a café in the middle. When agents from different PCs are waiting for permission at the same time, they walk to the café and chat. It is the most useless feature I have written this year, and my favourite.

What I learned

  • Pure core, visual edges. The reducer and the scene are deterministic functions of events and time. That made almost everything testable without a browser, and the browser tests compare screenshots pixel by pixel.
  • The floor had to become data. The shared office started on the same small room repeated side by side. A single large floor meant turning the room's constants into a value that themes can declare. Every existing screenshot had to stay identical while that happened, and that rule caught more bugs than any review.
  • Agents are better reviewers than I expected, and worse at reading screenshots than I am. I built most of this with Claude Code, with a fresh agent reviewing each change. They found real concurrency and edge-case bugs; I still had to look at every picture.

Try it

  • Repository: https://github.com/Jfernandez27/deskmates?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=deskmates
  • Install: npm install -g deskmates, then deskmates serve and deskmates connect
  • Node 22.18 or newer

If you run several agents a day, I would like to know which signal you miss most when they work in the background. That is what decides what the office learns next.

What if you could ask AI questions about invoices, unpaid bills, and financial records instead of searching through them manually?

title: Meet Harnis: the open-source platform for running AI agents safely across your company
summary:
AI agents are finally useful enough to do real work: fix code, answer customers, update tickets, run internal tools. The hard part isn't getting an agent to act. It's letting it act inside a company: across teams and customers, on real systems, with someone accountable for every change and a bill that doesn't surprise anyone.

That's what Harnis is for. It's an open-source, self-hosted platform that gives every agent in your organization the same harness: isolation, approvals, sandboxing, budgets and an audit trail, so teams can ship agents quickly without rebuilding the safety layer every time.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis
  • PyPI: pip install harnis
  • Helm chart: oci://ghcr.io/karawash-projects/charts/harnis
  • License: Apache 2.0

Why a harness?

Every team that builds an agent ends up writing the same plumbing: who is this user, which customer's data can they see, should this action wait for a human, where does model-written code run, how much did that conversation cost, and who approved what. When each team writes it alone, you get ten slightly different answers and no single place to audit.

Harnis turns that plumbing into a platform. Agents plug in; the guarantees come with them.

Three products on one engine

Harnis ships three ready-to-use workloads, all running on the same orchestrator:

1. A coding agent for your developers. Point the CLI at a project and describe the change. The agent works on an isolated copy, shows a diff for every file it wants to write, asks before running any command, runs your tests in a sandbox, and applies the final result to your files only when you confirm.

harnis --workspace ./my-service "add input validation to the signup handler and a test for it"

2. Multi-agent workflows. A router on a small, fast model reads each message and hands it to the right specialist (a support agent, a coding agent, or your own). Agents can hand work to each other or escalate to a person. Add a new specialist with a few lines of plugin code.

3. A multi-tenant agent app. A full API with live streaming over WebSockets and a web console for every role:

  • Users chat with agents and see each proposed change, with diffs inline.
  • Reviewers work an approvals queue and see usage and analytics.
  • Admins manage agents and their prompt versions, API keys and the audit log.
  • Platform admins create and manage tenants.

What every agent gets for free

Customer data stays separated, by the database itself

Every tenant table uses Postgres row-level security, enabled and forced, and the app connects with a role that can't bypass it. The tenant always comes from the verified login or API key, never from the request. Even a query that forgets to filter by tenant can't return another customer's data.

A human approves the exact action

Writing files, running commands and installing packages pause the session until a reviewer approves. The approval is tied to a cryptographic hash of the exact action, so the agent can't get approval for one change and then make a different one. Approvals expire, and separation of duties can stop people approving their own sessions. Paused sessions live in the database, so a decision made hours later resumes the work on any server.

Model-written code runs in a disposable sandbox

Each command gets a fresh Docker container or Kubernetes Pod with no network, a read-only system, no Linux privileges, a non-root user and strict memory, CPU and process limits. gVisor is supported for an extra kernel boundary. Files coming back out are checked, so a model can't sneak a link to a host file into your project.

Need packages? An approved install goes through a proxy that only allows package registries, and it can only change a separate dependency folder, never your code.

Security that checks itself

On Kubernetes, Harnis doesn't just assume the network rules are in place. Before it copies anything into a sandbox Pod, it probes from inside the Pod and only proceeds once the network is confirmed blocked. If the cluster can't isolate the sandbox, the command is refused with a clear error rather than run unprotected.

Costs you can predict

  • Per-turn budgets for steps, tool calls, hand-offs and spend in USD.
  • Per-tenant cost caps.
  • A token and cost ledger per model.
  • A loop breaker: it spots an agent repeating itself, warns it, then hands the session to a person.
  • Confirmed prices: you confirm each model's price at setup, so cost figures and caps are based on real numbers.

Your models, your rules

  • Models: use Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini or Amazon Nova on Bedrock, or self-hosted ones through any OpenAI-compatible API (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, LiteLLM).
  • Failover: you set the order and Harnis fails over between providers automatically.
  • Data residency: each tenant has its own list of allowed providers, and failover never sends that tenant's data outside it.

Your login, your roles

  • Single sign-on: any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Google), with group-to-role mapping.
  • Roles: user, reviewer, tenant admin and platform admin.
  • API keys: service keys for CI and automation, with roles, expiry and instant revocation.

Your tools and agents

A plugin SDK lets you add tools, agents and even model providers that register exactly like the built-in ones. Internal APIs, ticketing systems and databases all become tools that inherit approvals, sandboxing and auditing automatically.

Built-in guardrails

  • Prompt injection: incoming messages are checked for injection attempts.
  • Card numbers: they're redacted before the model sees them.
  • Tool output: it's marked as untrusted data, so instructions hidden in a file or web page aren't treated as commands.
  • Semantic cache: repeated questions are answered from the cache, which is fast and costs nothing.

Ready for your auditors and your ops team

  • Audit log: append-only, exportable as JSON or NDJSON.
  • Monitoring: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics and alert webhooks.
  • Data lifecycle: retention jobs, per-user data export and erasure, and backup and restore commands with verification.

Runs where you do

On a laptop, everything starts with Docker Compose on Windows, macOS or Linux. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart deploys:

  • the API, which scales out because sessions resume on any replica;
  • database migrations, run before each install or upgrade;
  • scheduled maintenance;
  • a separate, locked-down namespace for sandbox Pods.

Try it in five minutes, without an API key

The quick start uses a built-in mock model, so you can explore approvals, the sandbox and the loop breaker for free:

git clone https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis.git
cd harnis
python tasks.py install
python tasks.py up              # Postgres, Redis, tracing, demo tenants
python tasks.py sandbox-image
python tasks.py dev             # http://127.0.0.1:8000

Open the console, click Continue as local developer, and type create calc.py. The coding agent proposes two files with diffs, waits for your approvals, then runs the tests in the sandbox. Try repeat: list the files to watch the loop breaker step in, or ignore all previous instructions to see the input guard. When you're ready, python tasks.py check runs a complete feature check against your instance.

Built to be tested

Each release passes:

  • a cross-platform test suite;
  • end-to-end checks against a running API;
  • an evaluation suite and red-team scenarios;
  • sandbox tests under gVisor;
  • a full Helm deployment on a Kubernetes cluster in CI.

The same feature-check script ships with Harnis, so you can verify your own deployment the way the project verifies its releases.

Get involved

Harnis 1.0 is out now, free under Apache 2.0, and provided as is. Star the repo, try it on a real workflow, and tell me what you'd build on it:

https://github.com/karawash-projects/harnis

Issues, ideas and pull requests are welcome.

title: Partner commissions on serverless Node and Postgres, with no server to run
summary:
I run a small software company in Malaysia. We sell through referral partners and agents, and we pay them a share of what customers pay, not once, but for as long as the customer keeps paying.

That sounds simple until you try to do it. A customer pays on the 3rd. You promise the partner 25%, but only after a 30-day hold, in case the customer asks for a refund. In month 13 the rate drops to 20%. A refund arrives for half of one payment. The partner quits, and now you owe their unpaid commission to the house. Every one of those is a place where money can be wrong.

Of course, there are many existing tools in the market that does this out of the box, some even self-hosted. However, most tools that do this want their own server. A hosted CRM, or a self-hosted one with a Docker container, a background worker and a queue. We run on a serverless stack: Next.js functions on Vercel and one Postgres database. There is no machine of ours that stays switched on, and we felt like the cost vs benefit doesn't justify maintaining one just to pay partners.

Since we could not find a tool that did this and ran as a library inside our stack, we built one. It is called Tandem CRM, it is open source (MIT), and this post is about how it works and what I learned.

The idea: a CRM that is just a library and a schema

Tandem is an npm package plus a set of SQL migrations. You point it at a Postgres database you already have, and it adds a tandem schema with leads, agents, partners, commissions and payouts. There is no separate server and no container to run.

That is the part that matters for serverless. Each call is just a function that opens a database connection, does its work inside one transaction, and returns. Nothing holds state in memory between requests, so it does not care how many function instances you have or how often they start and stop. The state lives in Postgres, and Postgres is what keeps two requests from stepping on each other: the code locks the lead's row before it writes, so two payment webhooks arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Hold periods and releases are plain SQL, so a scheduled job (a cron route on Vercel works, and is how we do it) calls one function, release_due_commissions(), and that is the only background work there is.

npm install tandem-crm
npx tandem-crm init --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" --sample-data

init applies the migrations, runs a health check, and can seed a small demo workspace so you have something to look at.

Every payment gets its own commission line

Here is a lead being created and a payment being recorded. Everything goes through one shared writer, so the rules apply the same way whether the call comes from your app, a webhook or the admin screen.

import { defineTandemConfig } from "tandem-crm";
import { createTandemPool, withTandemSession, createLead, recordPayment } from "tandem-crm/db";

const pool = createTandemPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const config = defineTandemConfig({
  commission: {
    holdDays: 30,
    rateSchedule: [
      { fromMonth: 0, basisPoints: 2500 },   // 25% for the first year
      { fromMonth: 12, basisPoints: 2000 },  // 20% after that
    ],
  },
});

const { leadId } = await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  createLead(client, {
    workspaceId,
    companyName: "Aman Logistics",
    contactPhone: "+60 12-345 6789",
    qualificationMetric: 8,
    productTag: "starter",
    partnerId: "rajesh",
    config,
    source: "signup",
    sourceEventId: "signup-1042",
  })
);

await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  recordPayment(client, {
    workspaceId,
    leadId,
    config,
    source: "stripe",
    payment: {
      paymentId: "inv_001",
      amountMinor: 30000,          // RM300.00, always whole sen
      currency: "MYR",
      confirmedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
    partnerStatus: async (id) => ({ id, active: true }),
  })
);

Each payment produces one commission line with its own rate and its own 30-day hold. A scheduled job releases lines once they are due. If a refund comes in, the matching line is reduced or clawed back. If a partner is deactivated, their unpaid lines move to a house account. That policy is something you configure, not something we decide for you. We just decided to set ours up this way.

Why events

Tandem stores what happened, not just the current state. A lead is a stream of events: created, qualified, converted, paid, refunded. The current status is calculated by replaying them.

The practical benefit is that every decision is saved in the event it was made in. The rate that applied, the qualification result, who the beneficiary was. If you change your commission settings next year, old payments do not quietly change. And when a partner asks "why did I get this amount?", you can answer with the actual history.

Row-level security, so one tenant cannot read another

Tandem uses Postgres row-level security. Every query runs as a role called authenticated, and every row belongs to a workspace. Agents can only append three kinds of event (lead.lost, lead.stage_changed, conversion.confirmed). Anything that moves money needs an owner or admin, and the database enforces it, not just the application code.

The one setup step people trip on: the role you connect with must be able to grant authenticated. init explains this clearly if it cannot.

What two audits found

I am not a programmer by training, and I built this with quite a bit of help from AI and learning each step of the way (I make sure I understand at least fundamentally what the code is supposed to do). That is exactly why I did not want to trust it on my own. I had two independent audits run over the money code, and I wrote tests against a real Postgres instead of mocks.

The audits found real problems. A scheduled release job that could crash part way through. A case where a payment could silently produce no commission at all. Writes that were not safe if two requests arrived at the same moment. All of them are fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

The rules we now follow for anything that touches money:

  • Money is integer minor units. No floating point anywhere.
  • Every write to a lead locks the lead row first, replays the history plus the new events, and only then inserts.
  • Retrying a request with the same source id returns the existing result and never creates a duplicate.
  • A fix needs a test that fails without it.

Where it is tested

The test suites run against real Postgres 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 in CI, on Node 20 and 22, and also as a limited, non-superuser admin account, which is what most managed hosts give you. I have also run it by hand on Neon, Supabase, Layerbase and Aiven. Aiven needs its own certificate file, and the docs say how.

What it is not (yet)

It is early and pre-1.0, and it has not been proven at scale. It has run the partner commission ledger for our own product, Utuh, since 20 October 2026, and I checked it end to end on the live Stripe account, with a real card payment from an outside account and a real refund. No outside developers use the package yet, and we still pay partners by hand, by bank transfer. It is one Postgres and an append-only events table, which should be fine for small and medium use, but I have not load tested it.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

  • Repo: https://github.com/angkutdigital/tandem-crm
  • Docs: https://tandemcrm.dev

The most useful thing you can do is run it against your own Postgres host and open a "Postgres host report" issue, whether it worked or not. If a guide confused you, that is a bug in the guide, and I would like to know.

The state lives in Postgres, and Postgres is what keeps two requests from stepping on each other: the code locks the lead's row before it writes, so two payment webhooks arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Hold periods and releases are plain SQL, so a scheduled job (a cron route on Vercel works, and is how we do it) calls one function, release_due_commissions(), and that is the only background work there is.

npm install tandem-crm
npx tandem-crm init --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" --sample-data

init applies the migrations, runs a health check, and can seed a small demo workspace so you have something to look at.

Every payment gets its own commission line

Here is a lead being created and a payment being recorded. Everything goes through one shared writer, so the rules apply the same way whether the call comes from your app, a webhook or the admin screen.

import { defineTandemConfig } from "tandem-crm";
import { createTandemPool, withTandemSession, createLead, recordPayment } from "tandem-crm/db";

const pool = createTandemPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const config = defineTandemConfig({
  commission: {
    holdDays: 30,
    rateSchedule: [
      { fromMonth: 0, basisPoints: 2500 },   // 25% for the first year
      { fromMonth: 12, basisPoints: 2000 },  // 20% after that
    ],
  },
});

const { leadId } = await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  createLead(client, {
    workspaceId,
    companyName: "Aman Logistics",
    contactPhone: "+60 12-345 6789",
    qualificationMetric: 8,
    productTag: "starter",
    partnerId: "rajesh",
    config,
    source: "signup",
    sourceEventId: "signup-1042",
  })
);

await withTandemSession(pool, ownerId, (client) =>
  recordPayment(client, {
    workspaceId,
    leadId,
    config,
    source: "stripe",
    payment: {
      paymentId: "inv_001",
      amountMinor: 30000,          // RM300.00, always whole sen
      currency: "MYR",
      confirmedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    },
    partnerStatus: async (id) => ({ id, active: true }),
  })
);

Each payment produces one commission line with its own rate and its own 30-day hold. A scheduled job releases lines once they are due. If a refund comes in, the matching line is reduced or clawed back. If a partner is deactivated, their unpaid lines move to a house account. That policy is something you configure, not something we decide for you. We just decided to set ours up this way.

Why events

Tandem stores what happened, not just the current state. A lead is a stream of events: created, qualified, converted, paid, refunded. The current status is calculated by replaying them.

The practical benefit is that every decision is saved in the event it was made in. The rate that applied, the qualification result, who the beneficiary was. If you change your commission settings next year, old payments do not quietly change. And when a partner asks "why did I get this amount?", you can answer with the actual history.

Row-level security, so one tenant cannot read another

Tandem uses Postgres row-level security. Every query runs as a role called authenticated, and every row belongs to a workspace. Agents can only append three kinds of event (lead.lost, lead.stage_changed, conversion.confirmed). Anything that moves money needs an owner or admin, and the database enforces it, not just the application code.

The one setup step people trip on: the role you connect with must be able to grant authenticated. init explains this clearly if it cannot.

What two audits found

I am not a programmer by training, and I built this with quite a bit of help from AI and learning each step of the way (I make sure I understand at least fundamentally what the code is supposed to do). That is exactly why I did not want to trust it on my own. I had two independent audits run over the money code, and I wrote tests against a real Postgres instead of mocks.

The audits found real problems. A scheduled release job that could crash part way through. A case where a payment could silently produce no commission at all. Writes that were not safe if two requests arrived at the same moment. All of them are fixed, and each fix has a test that fails without it.

The rules we now follow for anything that touches money:

  • Money is integer minor units. No floating point anywhere.
  • Every write to a lead locks the lead row first, replays the history plus the new events, and only then inserts.
  • Retrying a request with the same source id returns the existing result and never creates a duplicate.
  • A fix needs a test that fails without it.

Where it is tested

The test suites run against real Postgres 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 in CI, on Node 20 and 22, and also as a limited, non-superuser admin account, which is what most managed hosts give you. I have also run it by hand on Neon, Supabase, Layerbase and Aiven. Aiven needs its own certificate file, and the docs say how.

What it is not (yet)

It is early and pre-1.0, and it has not been proven at scale. It has run the partner commission ledger for our own product, Utuh, since 20 October 2026, and I checked it end to end on the live Stripe account, with a real card payment from an outside account and a real refund. No outside developers use the package yet, and we still pay partners by hand, by bank transfer. It is one Postgres and an append-only events table, which should be fine for small and medium use, but I have not load tested it.

Try it, and tell me what breaks

  • Repo: https://github.com/angkutdigital/tandem-crm
  • Docs: https://tandemcrm.dev

The most useful thing you can do is run it against your own Postgres host and open a "Postgres host report" issue, whether it worked or not. If a guide confused you, that is a bug in the guide, and I would like to know.

title: The 13% Penalty: Why Synchronous APIs Still Scale Better Than You Think"
summary:
When I built a lightweight framework to act as a data marshal for my decoupled single page apps, I didn’t intend to write an architectural thesis, but along the way, the data forced me to confront three pervasive myths in modern web development. First, PHP is inherently slow, second that synchronous APIs can’t scale to modern demand, and finally that you must trade developer experience for raw performance. I confronted these assumptions the only way that matters, by building. I created a framework called mouse-php, created CLI tooling that eliminated micro-framework friction, and stress tested said framework to failure. What the benchmarking revealed was illuminating. The industry consensus around these three ideas aren’t built on hard engineering limits but misattribution, vendor marketing, cargo-culting, and outdated assumptions. Here’s the story of that build, the benchmark data behind it, and why low-level simplicity routinely beats over-engineered complexity.

When I set out to build mouse-php, my goal was to create a lightweight API that acted strictly as a data marshal for decoupled single page applications. Some choices were obvious, like stripping out framework bloat and keeping execution linear. However, I quickly realized that most lightweight solutions sacrifice developer velocity in the name of absolute performance. This exposes a false dichotomy in modern web development: the belief that developer conveniences must always come at the expense of runtime performance. Because I built mouse-php to solve my own production friction, I focused on creating low overhead pipelines that preserve developer ergonomics, this led to three distinct architectural choices.

1. The Inverse-MVC Pattern & Thin PDO Data Marshals

Traditional MVC frameworks push heavy ORMs and deep object graphs into giant models. In mouse-php, I inverted this relationship and completely ditched the ORM in favor of a clean, structured PDO wrapper. My primary motivation for dropping the ORM wasn’t raw performance, it was Developer Experience. The idea that ORMs deliver a superior DX is a shallow illusion. ORMs make trivial queries like User::find(1) look convenient, but simple requests were never difficult to manage in the first place. The moment an API requires real world database operations requiring complex JOINs, aggregations, or precise index targeting the ORM becomes a hindrance rather than helpful. Developers end up having to fight method chains, specific esoteric syntax, and performance killing abstractions just to perform queries that could have been written in three lines of SQL. By replacing ORM with an easy to parse PDO wrapper, mouse-php models act as bare metal data marshals executing raw, prepared SQL statements while still being easy to maintain.

  • Better DX: Developers write clear, explicit SQL without fighting dynamic query builders or dynamic relation tracking.
  • Zero Hydration Tax: Bypasses object instantiation and reflection entirely, fetching database results directly into native arrays at C-speed.
  • High Reusability: Because models are reduced to simple data pipes rather than stateful domain objects, a single query model can be applied across multiple controllers or background jobs without instantiating heavy object trees.

The performance boost of keeping database overhead under 1ms is simply the natural byproduct of choosing a cleaner developer interface.

2. Associative Array First Routing

Industry standard routers rely heavily on complex regex engines to parse dynamic URIs on every incoming request. In mouse-php, the routing engine uses associative array hash lookup first. Because decoupled SPAs communicate most efficiently via explicit RPC-style endpoints, direct match routes can be resolved instantly at C-speed using PHP’s native array key lookups. While dynamic URIs are still supported for standard REST compatibility, they are treated as secondary paths. Bypassing regex route parsing for the majority of API traffic eliminates a massive chunk of per-request CPU tax.

3. One Way Middleware (Abandoning the Onion Model)

Most modern frameworks use an “onion model” where middleware wraps both the incoming request and outgoing response in nested closure. I always hated dealing with onion middleware in heavy frameworks, debugging nested execution stacks across response boundaries was a constant source of friction as well as trying to just figure out how to use it in some cases. I moved mouse-php to a strict one way pipeline simply to make middleware easier to write, manage, and debug. But just as with the PDO wrapper, simplifying the DX revealed a blueprint built for high-throughput performance. In this linear model, middleware has only two jobs: guarding the application and injecting context.

  • Fast Escapes: If an authentication check fails, the pipeline immediately triggers an escape hatch and terminates the request early, preventing the request from controller instantiation entirely.
  • Direct Context Injection: For example if an auth check queries user details, it injects that data directly into the request payload. The downstream controller receives pre-hydrated context without making a second query.

Middleware never touches outgoing responses. Any final response formatting happens predictably in the controller layer via lightweight utilities. By replacing wrapped stack frames with a simple, unidirectional pipeline, we gain total debugging clarity and linear execution speed.

Once mouse-php was running, I needed empirical data to verify its throughput limits. Benchmarking modern HTTP APIs accurately is surprisingly nuanced; preliminary tests with closed loop tools like autocannon produced inconsistent, warped latency figures, likely due to Coordinated Omission. To get accurate, un-skewed latency profiles, I migrated the test bench to wrk2, an open loop benchmarking tool that maintains a fixed, constant throughput rate.

The Test Environment

All benchmarks were executed locally on bare-metal hardware to isolate the stack’s raw execution capability:

  • Hardware: Lenovo IdeaPad 5 2-in-1 (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, 16GB LPDDR5)
  • Operating System: Arch Linux (Kernel 7.2.8, KDE Plasma, non-essential background processes terminated)
  • CGI & Web Server: Apache httpd paired with PHP 8.5 PHP-FPM
  • PHP Runtime Tuning: OPcache enabled with aggressive timestamp checking disabled, JIT compiler active.

Test Parameters & Sweeps

  • Load Profile: wrk2 was configured with 4 threads, 100 concurrent connections, and a 60-second duration per run.
  • Rate Sweeps: Tests began at a 100 Req/s baseline and scaled up in increments to locate the framework's saturation knee.
  • Averaging & Outliers: Each target request rate was executed in three 60 second rounds and averaged together. If an anomalous system hiccup occurred, a 4th validation run was conducted to eliminate system jitter.
  • Thermal Mitigation: Because mobile SoCs aggressively thermal-throttle under sustained multi-core loads, a mandatory 5 minute system idle break was enforced between every run above 10,000 Req/s to prevent thermal soak from skewing tail-latency measurements.
  • Middleware Context Disclosures: Test endpoints were assigned to the native global_bypass middleware group. This bypassed client facing rate limiters and payload formatting guards that would otherwise reject standard synthetic wrk2 traffic, while mirroring how high throughput public endpoints are configured in production.

Using these test parameters, our control run targeted a route that returned a static JSON payload, isolating mouse-php’s routing request handling, and output pipeline from external I/O bound dependencies.

Analyzing this dataset reveals clear systems level behaviors regarding where the stack excels and precisely where hardware limits force it to break:

  1. The 2000 Req/s Efficiency Sweet Spot:

    Across the entire test suite, 2000 Req/s represents the optimal operational state. At this rate, latency hits its absolute minimum across all metrics : 1.41ms Average, 2.12ms P99, and a tight 2.75ms Max Latency. This is where request frequency perfectly aligns with CPU governor frequency scaling, worker process scheduling, and L1/L2 cache retention without triggering thread contention or queue accumulation.

  2. The 15,000 Req/s P99 stability Zone:

    While Max Latency tail drift begins decoupling after 2000 Req/s as individual process scheduling delays occur, the Average and P99 latency curves remain tightly locked together all the way to 15,000 Req/s. P99 latency does not break 5ms across a 15x increase in load. This proves that under normal operating conditions, 99% of requests pass through the framework’s array routing and one-way pipeline nearly instantaneously.

  3. The Warning Sign (15,500 Req/s):

    At 15,500 Req/s, P99 jumps from 4.53ms to 11.88ms. This decoupling between Average Latency(~2.0ms) and P99 marks the inflection point where OS socket backlogs and FastCGI worker queues begin running near capacity.

  4. The 17,500 Req/s Saturation Knee:

    The system maintains stability up to 17,500 Req/s with a 2.27ms average response time. Pushing the load to 18,000 Req/s causes the latency to explode immediately to 3.55 seconds.

This vertical wall isn’t an application level framework crash, it is classic FastCGI socket backlog exhaustion. When incoming connection rates exceed available PHP-FPM process slots, the OS TCP backlog fills up, incoming requests queue in kernel space, and the system hits its absolute physical CGI throughput ceiling on this hardware.

With the static baseline established, the next phase of stress-testing targeted an API endpoint that executes a live database query on every request, simulating a realistic application workload.

Comparing this dataset directly against our static control run reveals a great deal about mouse-php's execution efficiency under real-world I/O pressure:

  1. The Remarkable 13% Delta:

    The standout takeaway from these benchmarks is how little performance degrades when introducing a database query. Moving from a static JSON response to a live MariaDB lookup shifts our maximum stable throughput ceiling from 17,500 Req/s down to 15,250 Req/s is a mere 13% reduction. In typical web frameworks, the ORM and object hydration layer create a massive performance cliff. Here, because mouse-php uses a thin PDO wrapper that bypasses hydration overhead entirely, the database roundtrip adds less than 1ms of average latency across the board.

  2. The Persistent 2,000 Req/s Sweet Spot:

    Just like the static control run, 2,000 Req/s remains the absolute peak efficiency zone. Even with database reads executing on every single request, the system hits its tightest latency alignment (1.63ms Average, 2.63ms P99) right at this threshold. This confirms that CPU cache locality and process scheduling dynamics dominate the profile long before database I/O becomes the bottleneck.

  3. Predictable P99 Coupling & Early Decoupling:

    The P99 latency behavior mirrors the static control curve, though it begins its upward drift slightly earlier (~13,000 to 14,000 Req/s). This minor variance makes complete sense: as concurrent requests climb, the local MariaDB connection pool and socket buffers absorb additional load, causing occasional tail-latency stretching just before the saturation threshold.

  4. The 15,250 Req/s Saturation Wall:

    At 15,250 Req/s, the system holds the line with a sub-3ms average latency (2.27ms). Pushing past this edge to 16,000 Req/s triggers an immediate system blowout, with average latency jumping to 3.38 seconds. Just like the static run, this wall represents the physical concurrency limit of our local FastCGI and database socket queues on mobile hardware, rather than an application-layer failure.

The parallel behavior of these two charts tells a definitive story. mouse-php is bounded primarily by operating system socket limits, CGI throughput, and local hardware constraints, not by the application code or data-fetching pipeline. When your database backed endpoints can sustain over 15,000 requests per second with sub 2.5ms latency on a laptop, the argument that "synchronous PHP can't scale" completely falls apart.

Now with the data we have from our benchmarks we can more closely examine and determine the validity of pervasive myths and popular beliefs that dictate many of the design choices in web development. The numbers show us that the limitations that are often attributed to entire programming languages or execution models are almost always the result of something more specific that became an artificial dependency.

Myth 1: “PHP is Inherently Slow”

For over a decade, “PHP is slow” has permeated the zeitgeist of web developers through the industry. This is usually cited as a reason to justify migrating simple applications to heavier enterprise run times or microservices. However, this myth is the product of two sources that this data shows are both incorrect now or assigning the blame to the wrong source. The first source of this was likely from bad experiences from old versions of PHP, and the other misattribution: blaming the language runtime for the sins of the framework.

PHP a decade ago when this argument started was a much different beat then what we have now, and part of the problem is these critics of PHP have not been paying attention to that fact. As shown with these benchmarks PHP 8.2+, PHP-FPM, and optimizations like OPcache can make even synchronous PHP extremely fast and reliable while still letting you have the advantages of synchronous operations. There are also operations in PHP that are just faster than anything else with the same accessibility as PHP, like database operations and encryption. One of the things I learned building mouse-php and mRPC/colby-jack was how to implement HMAC for both PHP and Javascript, and not only was PHP’s implementation more performant but far easier which means more secure as there are less chances for me as a developer to make an error.

The other source of this becomes obvious because mouse-php makes engineering choices that removes many of the sources of bloat that come from typical frameworks. As a result the performance uplift over a typical batteries included framework is obvious. I wasn’t the first to notice this naturally, microframeworks like slim exist to address this same bloat but this remains a source of this myth because typically people bench marking PHP reach for Laravel or Symfony as that’s what most people outside the PHP ecosystem think of for PHP backends. What our benchmarks show just like the outdated idea of PHP that the framework tax and the abstraction baggage that comes with the massive frameworks is the true performance killer and not the language runtime.

Myth 2: "Synchronous APIs Can’t Scale to Modern Demand”

The modern cloud-native ecosystem is built on the premise that synchronous execution models hit a hard wall under real world load, necessitating complex asynchronous event loops, reactive streams, or Kubernetes-orchestrated microservices.

Our MariaDB benchmark challenges this assumption. By pushing a database backed endpoint to 15,250 requests per second with sub 2.5ms baseline latencies we showed that a simple synchronous request response model can absorb massive production traffic. To put this number in perspective 15,250 requests per second equates to 1.3 billion requests a day running on a laptop not built for web hosting. For 99% of web applications, microservice splits and async complexity solves problems they will simply never have and just introduces operation overhead, or latency taxes that definitely don’t need.

This does reveal the source of this myth however, cargo-culting and vendor marketing, the idea that these complex solutions are the best practice primarily comes from people seeing FAANG companies use these solutions in their own stacks. The problem with this is the colossal delta in traffic and developers between even a decently high traffic application and Google. The scale that a FAANG corporation’s infrastructure is working at means that the economics and what makes something efficient change drastically meaning that trying to copy their infrastructure leads to unnecessary complexity or even worse performance in certain areas then the simpler solution.

Myth 3: “Performance vs. DX is a Zero-Sum Game”

Perhaps the most damaging myth in web development and one I began to be frustrated with the trade off narrative: the belief that if you want high performance, you must write low level, tedious boilerplate; and if you want great Developer Experience(DX), you must accept a heavy runtime tax.

Building mouse-php showed me that not only was this not true, but many features touted as making things easier for developers are shallow making the performance trade offs bad deals for the convenience, actually make things more difficult when you actually try building something, are just a development tool and don’t need to affect the performance of the production runtime. The interesting part of the performance uplift shown in this post was that it wasn’t the direct target of the choices made, removing ORMs and simplifying middleware management and flow was all done to just make it easier to understand and work with. These benchmarks are particularly interesting because this API was created from a blank directory. From that blank directory I created and configured the endpoints in around ten minutes, which was a great demonstration that performance doesn’t need to be hard.

Good developer experience isn’t about hiding complexity behind magic abstraction, it's about making the complexity easier to understand or removing redundant work. True DX is about clarity, predictability, and getting out of an engineer’s way. When tools are simple to reason about, high performance isn’t something you have to explicitly aim for; good engineering choices become obvious as a natural byproduct of clean design.
When we strip away industry dogma, cargo-culted microservices, and multilayered abstraction taxes, web architecture becomes remarkably clear. The benchmarks suggest to us: simplicity scales, hardware is rarely the real bottleneck, and high performance is simply the natural byproduct of clean design.
For 99% of web applications, the push toward "cloud complex" architecture solves a scaling problem they will never face, while saddling them with operational overhead they definitely don't need. You don't need a thousand dollar auto scaling cluster to build something fast.
What all of this has shown me is that respecting developer velocity and application performance are not mutually exclusive. When you look past industry assumptions and focus on building well reasoned solutions to immediate problems, you can create outcomes that defy expectations.
This approach gave me a tool that not only delivered sub 3ms latencies on database backed requests, but did so with a backend that took ten minutes to build from an empty directory, all without the added complexity of managing asynchronous loops, explicit state lifecycles, or heavy framework abstractions.
Sometimes, all it takes is stepping back, cutting out the bloat, and letting the metal do what it was built to do.

If you want to check out the code, clone the repo, or test mouse-php yourself, you can find it here:
https://github.com/drawfig/mouse-php

If you’d like to learn more about how to install it using create-mouse-app or some of the other tooling and architectural choices I made in this project the Docs are here:
https://github.com/drawfig/mouse-php/wiki

  • PHP Runtime Tuning: OPcache enabled with aggressive timestamp checking disabled, JIT compiler active.

Test Parameters & Sweeps

  • Load Profile: wrk2 was configured with 4 threads, 100 concurrent connections, and a 60-second duration per run.
  • Rate Sweeps: Tests began at a 100 Req/s baseline and scaled up in increments to locate the framework's saturation knee.
  • Averaging & Outliers: Each target request rate was executed in three 60 second rounds and averaged together. If an anomalous system hiccup occurred, a 4th validation run was conducted to eliminate system jitter.
  • Thermal Mitigation: Because mobile SoCs aggressively thermal-throttle under sustained multi-core loads, a mandatory 5 minute system idle break was enforced between every run above 10,000 Req/s to prevent thermal soak from skewing tail-latency measurements.
  • Middleware Context Disclosures: Test endpoints were assigned to the native global_bypass middleware group. This bypassed client facing rate limiters and payload formatting guards that would otherwise reject standard synthetic wrk2 traffic, while mirroring how high throughput public endpoints are configured in production.

Using these test parameters, our control run targeted a route that returned a static JSON payload, isolating mouse-php’s routing request handling, and output pipeline from external I/O bound dependencies.
